usage: polite present; the most common spoken form
to feel a weight off one's chest
set phrase; literally 'the insides feel clear' — say this after venting or finishing something
adverb form, e.g. 후련하게 울다 to have a good cleansing cry
-아/어지다 shows the shift from heavy to light
examples: 할 말을 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련하네요.
Now that I've said everything I wanted to, I feel so relieved.
the classic context: after finally speaking your mind
시험 끝나서 진짜 후련해요.
I'm so relieved the exam is finally over.
use it when a stressful thing is done, not just when you're happy
밀린 설거지 다 했더니 후련하다.
I did all the piled-up dishes and now I feel refreshed.
casual 해라체 ending; works for clearing any backlog
nuance: 후련하다 is the clean, lightened feeling you get right after a burden or stress is released — finishing exams, finally venting, crying it out. It is not general happiness; it specifically implies something heavy was weighing on you and now it's gone. Pair it with 속이 to talk about emotional release.
mistakes: Don't use 후련하다 for plain happiness — it requires a preceding burden or stress that has just been lifted.
It is not interchangeable with 시원하다 for physical coolness; 후련하다 is about emotional/internal release (though 속이 시원하다 overlaps).

english: uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling
usage: polite present; common after an awkward or unresolved moment
뭔가 ('somehow/something') is the usual partner word
adverb form, e.g. 찝찝하게 헤어졌어요 we parted on an unsettled note
examples: 아까 그렇게 말한 게 좀 찝찝해요.
I feel a bit uneasy about how I said that earlier.
lingering regret about your own words or actions
사과는 받았는데 뭔가 찝찝하네요.
I got an apology, but something still feels off.
when a resolution doesn't fully satisfy you
손 안 씻고 밥 먹으려니까 찝찝해.
Eating without washing my hands feels icky.
also works for literal not-quite-clean physical discomfort
nuance: 찝찝하다 is that nagging, not-quite-resolved discomfort — a conversation that ended badly, a decision you're not sure about, or even a slightly unclean feeling. It's milder than guilt or anxiety; it's the residue that sticks with you. Very common in casual speech; the spelling 찜찜하다 is also accepted but 찝찝하다 is more frequent online.
mistakes: Don't confuse it with 불안하다 (anxious about the future) — 찝찝하다 is about an unresolved feeling lingering from something that already happened.
Avoid it in formal writing or business contexts; it reads as casual and a little slangy.

english: overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle
usage: polite present; context decides positive vs negative
set phrase for being moved/overcome by joy or pride
attributive form; common with 감동, 행복
adverb form, e.g. 벅차게 다가오다 to hit one overwhelmingly
examples: 첫 월급을 받으니까 가슴이 벅차네요.
Getting my first paycheck, my heart just swells.
the positive 'overcome with emotion' sense
혼자 하기엔 일이 좀 벅차요.
This is a bit too much for me to handle alone.
the practical sense: a task exceeds your capacity
벅찬 하루였어요.
It was an overwhelming day.
can mean emotionally moving OR exhausting depending on tone
nuance: 벅차다 has two flavors: the heart-swelling kind (overcome with joy, pride, gratitude) and the practical kind (a workload or responsibility that's too much for you). With 가슴이 it's almost always the emotional, positive sense. Listen to context to tell which one a speaker means.
mistakes: Don't assume 벅차다 is always positive — '일이 벅차다' means a task is overwhelming in a stressful, can't-cope way.
It is not the same as 바쁘다 (busy); 벅차다 implies the amount exceeds your capacity, not just that you have a lot to do.

english: empty; feeling a void; missing something
usage: to feel a void in one's heart
set phrase for loneliness or loss
adverb form, e.g. 집이 허전하게 느껴져요 the house feels empty
examples: 룸메이트가 이사 가니까 집이 너무 허전해요.
Now that my roommate moved out, the place feels so empty.
the void left when someone or something is gone
머리 자르고 나니까 목이 허전하네요.
After the haircut, my neck feels bare.
also used for a physical 'something's missing' feeling
뭔가 허전해서 자꾸 핸드폰을 찾게 돼요.
Something feels missing, so I keep reaching for my phone.
that restless 'incomplete' sensation
nuance: 허전하다 is the quiet emptiness left behind when something or someone is missing — a friend moves away, a routine ends, or you just feel a vague void. It's gentler and more wistful than 외롭다 (lonely); it can attach to a place, a body part (느낌), or your heart. Often paired with 마음이 or 뭔가.
mistakes: Don't equate it with 슬프다 (sad) — 허전하다 is about absence and a hollow feeling, not active sorrow.
외롭다 is specifically about being alone; 허전하다 can apply even when people are around but something familiar is gone.

usage: polite present; very common compliment-adjacent word
set phrase; you feel backed-up and safe
attributive form; high praise for a friend or colleague
adverb form, e.g. 든든하게 먹다 to eat a hearty meal
examples: 네가 옆에 있으니까 진짜 든든하다.
Having you by my side is so reassuring.
warm thing to say to a close friend or partner
아침 든든하게 먹고 나왔어요.
I had a hearty breakfast before heading out.
the 'pleasantly full and fueled' sense
통장에 비상금 있으니까 마음이 든든해요.
Having emergency savings makes me feel secure.
reassurance from having a reliable backup
nuance: 든든하다 is the warm feeling of being backed up and secure — a dependable friend, a safety net, or a filling meal that sets you up for the day. Calling someone 든든하다 is a real compliment about reliability. With food it means satisfyingly full and energized, not just 'not hungry'.
mistakes: Don't use 배부르다 when you mean a hearty, fueling meal — 든든하게 먹다 carries the nuance of being well-prepared, not just full.
It describes reassurance you feel, so say 마음이 든든하다 / 사람이 든든하다, not 'I am 든든해' to mean you yourself are reliable in the abstract.

english: light and unburdened; free of a load
usage: polite present; said when a responsibility ends
adverb form, e.g. 홀가분하게 떠나다 to leave unburdened
examples: 프로젝트 끝나서 마음이 홀가분해요.
The project's over, so I feel light and free.
the relief of shedding a long responsibility
짐 다 부치고 홀가분하게 여행 다녔어요.
I shipped all my luggage and traveled light and carefree.
literal lightness blending into emotional lightness
빚 다 갚으니까 진짜 홀가분하다.
Now that I've paid off all my debt, I feel truly unburdened.
casual ending; releasing a long-carried weight
nuance: 홀가분하다 is the lightness you feel after putting down a long-carried load — finishing a big project, paying off debt, ending an obligation. It overlaps with 후련하다 but emphasizes freedom from a burden rather than the release of stress; you feel free to move, not just relieved. Often paired with 마음이.
mistakes: Don't use it for momentary relief — 홀가분하다 implies a lasting burden has finally been set down for good.
It's close to 후련하다 but not identical: 후련하다 = the cathartic release; 홀가분하다 = the resulting freedom and lightness.

usage: polite present; describes the relationship's distance
attributive form; 사이 = the relationship between people
adverb form, e.g. 서먹하게 인사하다 to greet stiffly
examples: 오랜만에 만나니까 좀 서먹하네요.
Meeting after so long, things feel a little awkward.
distance that builds up after time apart
같은 팀이지만 아직 서먹해요.
We're on the same team, but it's still awkward between us.
not-yet-close coworkers
싸운 뒤로 둘이 서먹해졌어요.
The two of them grew distant after the fight.
-아/어지다 shows a relationship turning cold
nuance: 서먹하다 describes the awkward, not-yet-comfortable distance between people who aren't close — new coworkers, friends after a long gap, or two people after an argument. It's about interpersonal coolness, not personal embarrassment. The reduplicated 서먹서먹하다 is very common and a touch more vivid.
mistakes: Don't use it for self-conscious embarrassment — that's 어색하다/멋쩍다. 서먹하다 is specifically the distance between two parties.
It needs a relationship context; you can't be 서먹하다 by yourself — it's always 'between' people (둘이 서먹하다).

english: displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving
usage: polite present; expresses disapproval of something
attributive form; very common with 표정/얼굴/눈빛
adverb form, e.g. 못마땅하게 쳐다보다 to glare disapprovingly
examples: 부장님이 제 보고서를 못마땅해하셨어요.
The manager was displeased with my report.
use 못마땅해하다 when describing someone else's displeasure
뭐가 그렇게 못마땅한데?
What are you so unhappy about?
casual; said when someone is clearly grumbling
엄마는 내 결정이 못마땅한 표정이셨어요.
Mom had a disapproving look about my decision.
the classic 'disapproving face' collocation
nuance: 못마땅하다 means something doesn't sit right with you — you disapprove or find it unsatisfactory. It's often shown through facial expression (못마땅한 표정) rather than stated outright, and frequently involves a senior person reacting to a junior's choices. When describing a third person's feeling, use 못마땅해하다.
mistakes: When the displeased one is someone else, you must say 못마땅해하다 — Korean adjectives of feeling need -아/어하다 for third-person description.
Don't confuse it with 화나다 (angry); 못마땅하다 is quieter disapproval or dissatisfaction, not active anger.

usage: I'm displeased / I'm in a bad mood
polite present; the ㅎ of the ㄶ batchim drops, so it's pronounced [언짜나요]
to be in a sour mood
set phrase; 기분이 is the usual subject
attributive form; 기색 = visible sign of a feeling
adverb form, e.g. 언짢게 듣다 to take something the wrong way
examples: 제 말 때문에 기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송해요.
I'm sorry if what I said put you in a bad mood.
a polite, common way to apologize for offending someone
아침부터 무슨 일 있었는지 언짢아 보여요.
You look displeased — did something happen this morning?
noticing someone else's sour mood; -아/어 보이다 = looks
그 말투가 좀 언짢았어요.
That tone rubbed me the wrong way.
past tense; reacting to something mildly offensive
nuance: 언짢다 describes being in a displeased, slightly offended, sour mood — the way you feel when something rubs you wrong but you're not full-on angry. It's a notch more personal and mood-focused than 못마땅하다, and it appears constantly in polite apologies ('기분 언짢으셨다면'). Remember the silent ㄶ batchim in pronunciation.
mistakes: Don't write it 언잖다 — the correct spelling is 언짢다 with ㄶ, even though the ㅎ is not clearly pronounced.
It's milder than 화나다; use 언짢다 for a soured mood or mild offense, not for real anger.

usage: polite present; a gentle, satisfied warmth
attributive form; very common with 미소/표정
set phrase; the prototypical action with this feeling
adverb form modifying verbs like 보다, 웃다
examples: 아이들 노는 거 보니까 흐뭇하네요.
Watching the kids play, I feel so warm inside.
the classic context: contentment watching others
후배가 잘 커서 흐뭇해요.
My junior has grown so capable — it makes me proud and happy.
warm pride at someone else's growth
흐뭇한 미소를 지으셨어요.
He gave a contented smile.
describing the gentle smile this feeling produces
nuance: 흐뭇하다 is a warm, gentle contentment — the soft satisfaction of watching something turn out well, especially others doing well (kids playing, a junior succeeding). It's tender and a little proud, not excited or thrilled. It pairs naturally with 미소 (smile) and 바라보다 (look on), since it's often a feeling you wear on your face.
mistakes: Don't use it for your own exciting achievements — 흐뭇하다 is calm, warm satisfaction, often directed at others or at a pleasing outcome.
When describing someone else's contentment, use 흐뭇해하다 (e.g. 부모님이 흐뭇해하셨어요).

english: deeply moved; choked up with emotion
usage: polite present; a sudden welling of emotion
set phrase; the most common form
vivid set phrase for nearly tearing up
adverb form, e.g. 뭉클하게 다가오다 to hit one emotionally
examples: 부모님 편지 읽고 가슴이 뭉클했어요.
Reading my parents' letter, I got all choked up.
the prototypical heartfelt context
그 장면이 너무 뭉클하더라고요.
That scene was so deeply moving.
-더라고요 reports a touching experience you had
오랜만에 본 친구 얼굴에 코끝이 뭉클했다.
Seeing my friend's face after so long, I got teary.
casual ending; that nose-tingling pre-tears feeling
nuance: 뭉클하다 is the sudden lump-in-your-throat, heart-swelling feeling of being deeply moved — a heartfelt letter, a reunion, a touching scene. It's warmer and more tender than just 감동하다 (to be impressed/moved); 뭉클 captures the physical welling-up sensation. Pair it with 가슴이 or the very evocative 코끝이.
mistakes: Don't use it for intellectual admiration — 뭉클하다 is the emotional, almost-teary physical reaction, not 'impressive'.
It describes a momentary surge, not a lasting state; you feel 뭉클하다 in a touching instant, then it passes.

usage: set phrase for the awkward laugh you give when embarrassed
-아/어하다 form to describe someone else looking sheepish
examples: 칭찬을 받으니까 좀 멋쩍었어요.
Getting complimented made me feel a bit sheepish.
the classic trigger: praise you don't know how to take
할 말이 없어서 멋쩍게 웃었어요.
I had nothing to say, so I just laughed sheepishly.
the awkward-laugh reflex
사람들 앞에서 넘어져서 멋쩍더라고요.
I tripped in front of everyone and felt so self-conscious.
mild public embarrassment, not deep shame
nuance: 멋쩍다 is that mild, sheepish self-consciousness — being complimented, caught in a small slip, or stuck with nothing to say, so you give an awkward little laugh. It's lighter than 부끄럽다 (shy/ashamed) and is about your own social awkwardness in the moment. The phrase 멋쩍게 웃다 (laugh sheepishly) is extremely common.
mistakes: Don't spell it 멋적다 — the standard spelling is 멋쩍다.
It's about your own sheepishness, unlike 서먹하다 which is the distance between two people; don't swap them.
